source_text:
Fragmentum in epistulam ad Philemonem (in catenis)
Phm
1,1 Ἐν πολλαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ξένον τίθησι ῥῆμα τοῦ μέλλοντος εἰσάγεσθαι λόγου
κατασκευαστικόν, καὶ νῦν ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ–
ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν.
thought_title: Paul's unusual word prepares his appeal
orientation: Photius is commenting on Philemon 1:1, explaining how Paul's opening word prepares for his appeal on behalf of Onesimus.
pass_a_gloss: In many letters he places an unusual word preparatory of the argument about to be introduced, and now since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus by his own standing—and his standing is being in chains—he shows the credibility of the appeal.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'unusual word' for ξένον ῥῆμα; keeps the noun phrase natural in English.
Glossary requires 'preparatory' for κατασκευαστικόν; it modifies the unusual word as serving to prepare the coming argument.
Glossary requires 'standing' for ἀξία; it denotes Paul's worth or status, not moral merit.
Glossary requires 'being in chains' for τὸ δεδέσθαι; it renders the perfect passive infinitive as a state of imprisonment.
Glossary requires 'credibility' for ἀξιόπιστον; it names the trustworthiness of the appeal.
Glossary requires 'appeal' for παράκλησις; it is Paul's request on behalf of Onesimus, not comfort or exhortation.

bible_refs.note: The fragment comments on Philemon 1:1; no direct quotation of the verse wording is present in this section.

pass_b_english: In many letters Paul places an unusual word as preparation for the argument he is about to introduce. Here too, since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, he does so on the basis of his own standing—and his standing is being in chains. In this way he shows the credibility of his appeal.

last_rejected.why: 'καὶ νῦν' means 'and now', not 'here too'; changes temporal sense.
last_rejected.fix: And now, since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus...
last_rejected.ruling: καὶ νῦν ('and now') idiomatically means 'here too' in context; no meaning lost, just standard rendering.
